q: Which country is traditionally the home of pizza?
x: Modern pizza took shape in Naples, where flatbreads with tomato became a cheap street food in the 1700s and 1800s.

q: Which country is sushi traditionally associated with?
x: The word sushi refers to the vinegared rice, not the fish. The dish began as a way of preserving fish in fermented rice.

q: What fruit is the main ingredient of guacamole?
x: The name comes from the Aztec Nahuatl word ahuacamolli, which roughly means 'avocado sauce'.

q: Which fruit is dried to make raisins?
x: Raisins are traditionally sun-dried. Sultanas and currants are also dried grapes, just of different varieties.

q: What is tofu made from?
x: Tofu is made by curdling soy milk and pressing the curds into blocks, much like making cheese.

q: Which country is feta cheese traditionally from?
x: Traditional feta is brined and made mostly from sheep's milk, sometimes mixed with goat's milk.

q: What sweet food do bees make from flower nectar?
x: Bees fan the nectar with their wings to evaporate water, and enzymes turn it into honey stored in the comb.

q: Which legume is the main ingredient in hummus?
x: Hummus is the Arabic word for chickpeas. The dip is blended with tahini, lemon juice and garlic.

q: Which costly spice consists of the dried stigmas of a crocus flower?
x: Each crocus flower gives just three stigmas, all picked by hand, which is why saffron is so expensive.

q: Which Italian dish layers flat pasta sheets with meat sauce and bechamel?
x: The word lasagna may come from the Greek lasanon, meaning a cooking pot, or from the Latin lasanum.

q: Which nut is the main ingredient of marzipan?
x: Marzipan is a paste of ground almonds and sugar, often shaped into tiny fruits or used to cover cakes.

q: Which country is the long, thin baguette a symbol of?
x: A French decree in 1993 set rules for the 'traditional baguette': only flour, water, salt and yeast.

q: Which gas, made by yeast, makes bread dough rise?
x: Yeast ferments sugars in the dough and releases carbon dioxide, which gets trapped in the gluten and puffs up the loaf.

q: Which vegetable is fermented to make sauerkraut?
x: Sauerkraut means 'sour cabbage' in German. Sailors ate it on long voyages because it kept well.

q: What is the dried seaweed sheet used to wrap sushi rolls called?
x: Nori is made by shredding red algae and pressing it into sheets, much like making paper, then toasting it.

q: Which seeds are roasted and ground to make chocolate?
x: Cacao beans are the seeds of a fruit that grows straight from the trunk and branches of the cacao tree.

q: What is the Italian word for ice cream?
x: Gelato is churned slowly, so it holds less air than American ice cream, and is served a little warmer.

q: Which vegetable is famous for making eyes water when it is cut?
x: Cutting an onion releases a sulfur gas that reacts with the moisture in your eyes and irritates them.

q: Which grain is the staple food of much of Asia?
x: Rice has been farmed for thousands of years, and in many Asian languages the word for rice also means 'meal'.

q: Which country is the traditional home of kimchi?
x: Kimchi is fermented vegetables, most often napa cabbage, seasoned with chili, garlic and ginger.

q: Which kitchen tool is commonly used to flip pancakes?
x: A thin, flexible spatula slides under delicate foods without tearing them.

q: Which kitchen tool do you use to drain boiled pasta?
x: A colander is a bowl full of holes. The word comes from the Latin colare, meaning 'to strain'.

q: Which tool is used to roll dough out flat?
x: Rolling pins can be wood, marble, glass or steel. Some bakers even chill them for flakier pastry.

q: Which vegetable are French fries made from?
x: Belgians and French both claim the fry. In the United States they are called French fries, in Britain they are chips.

q: Which fruit wears its seeds on the outside of its skin?
x: A strawberry has roughly 200 tiny seeds on its surface. Each one is really a separate little fruit.

q: Which Mexican flatbread is made from corn or wheat flour?
x: Corn tortillas date back to the Aztecs and earlier, who made the dough from corn treated with lime.

q: Which Indian flatbread is traditionally baked in a clay oven called a tandoor?
x: Naan dough is stuck to the hot wall of the tandoor, where it puffs up and blisters in minutes.

q: Which Spanish rice dish is traditionally colored and flavored with saffron?
x: The word paella also names the wide, shallow pan the dish is cooked in over an open fire.

q: Which creamy Italian rice dish is stirred slowly while hot broth is added?
x: Risotto rice releases starch as it is stirred, which gives the dish its creamy texture without any cream.

q: Which popular drink comes from steeping leaves in hot water and is often served with lemon?
x: After water, tea is said to be the most widely drunk beverage in the world.

q: Which country is famous for maple syrup and has a maple leaf on its flag?
x: Maple sap is boiled until most of its water has evaporated. Quebec is the biggest syrup-making region.

q: Which herb is the main ingredient in Genoese pesto?
x: Classic pesto also contains pine nuts, garlic, olive oil and hard cheese, crushed together in a mortar.

q: Which cheese is traditionally melted on a Margherita pizza?
x: Mozzarella is a stretchy cheese. Its name comes from the Italian verb mozzare, meaning 'to cut off'.

q: Which meat is traditionally used to make bacon?
x: Bacon is usually cut from the belly or back of a pig and then cured with salt and often smoked.

q: Which Japanese noodle soup is topped with sliced pork and a soft egg?
x: Ramen's wheat noodles came to Japan from China. Regional broths include miso, soy sauce and pork bone.

q: Which country is pho, a beef noodle soup, from?
x: Pho is traditionally eaten at breakfast in Vietnam, with fresh herbs, lime and bean sprouts on the side.

q: Which country is the traditional home of the taco?
x: A taco is just a tortilla wrapped around a filling. Tacos al pastor were inspired by Lebanese immigrants' shawarma.

q: Which vitamin are oranges especially well known for?
x: Sailors once carried citrus fruit on long voyages to prevent scurvy, a disease caused by a lack of vitamin C.

q: Which mineral, found in milk and cheese, is important for strong bones?
x: About 99 percent of the body's calcium is stored in the bones and teeth.

q: Which animal does mutton come from?
x: Mutton comes from an adult sheep. Meat from a young sheep is called lamb.

q: What is meat from a young calf called?
x: Veal is paler and more tender than beef. Wiener schnitzel is traditionally made from it.

q: Venison is meat from which animal?
x: The word venison comes from the Latin venari, meaning 'to hunt'.

q: Which fried chickpea ball is a popular street food across the Middle East?
x: Falafel is often stuffed into pita bread with salad and tahini sauce.

q: Which country is traditionally famous for fondue, a pot of melted cheese?
x: The word fondue is French for 'melted'. Diners dip bread cubes on long forks into a shared pot.

q: Edam and Gouda cheeses come from which country?
x: Both cheeses are named after Dutch towns. Edam is usually sold in a ball coated in red wax.

q: What is the yellow center of an egg called?
x: The yolk holds most of an egg's fat and vitamins, while the white is mostly protein and water.

q: Real mozzarella di bufala is made from the milk of which animal?
x: Italian water buffalo milk is richer than cow's milk, which gives the cheese its creamy flavor.

q: Which compound makes chili peppers taste hot?
x: Capsaicin is concentrated in the white ribs inside the pepper, not in the seeds themselves.

q: Vanilla is the seed pod of which type of flower?
x: Vanilla is the only edible fruit that comes from the orchid family, which has more than 25,000 species.

q: Which hot drink is made from ground roasted beans and served as espresso or latte?
x: Coffee beans are really seeds from the cherry-like fruit of the coffee plant.

q: Which Italian coffee drink has equal parts espresso, steamed milk and milk foam?
x: The drink is named after Capuchin friars, whose brown robes resembled the color of the coffee.

q: In Italian cooking, what does 'al dente' mean when applied to pasta?
x: Al dente literally means 'to the tooth'. Pasta cooked this way also digests more slowly than soft pasta.

q: What is it called to cook food gently in liquid just below boiling point?
x: A simmer shows small, slow bubbles at the surface, while a full boil bubbles vigorously.

q: Which tropical fruit is known for its spiky husk and very strong smell?
x: Durian smells so pungent that it is banned from many hotels and public transport in Southeast Asia.

q: Which fruit is filled with ruby-red, juicy seeds called arils?
x: A single pomegranate can hold several hundred arils, each wrapped around one seed.

q: Traditional caviar is the salted roe of which fish?
x: The best-known caviar comes from sturgeon in the Caspian and Black Seas.

q: Which orange root vegetable is rich in beta-carotene?
x: The body turns beta-carotene into vitamin A. Carrots were originally purple or yellow before orange ones were bred.

q: Which Italian dumplings are traditionally made from potato and flour?
x: Gnocchi are boiled until they float to the surface and are served with sauce or butter.

q: Which country is famous for haggis, a savory pudding of sheep offal and oats?
x: Haggis is traditionally served on Burns Night with mashed turnips and potatoes.

q: Which country is known for the classic dish of battered fish and fried potatoes?
x: Fish and chip shops spread across Britain in the 1860s, and the dish became a staple of working-class meals.

q: Which dairy product is made by churning cream?
x: Churning breaks up the fat globules in cream until they clump together, leaving buttermilk behind.

q: Which dairy food is made by fermenting milk with live bacterial cultures?
x: The bacteria turn milk's lactose into lactic acid, which thickens the milk and gives yogurt its tang.

q: Which ingredient makes up the bulk of most bread dough?
x: Bread flour contains more protein than cake flour, which helps build a strong, chewy structure.

q: What spicy green paste is traditionally served with sushi?
x: Much of the wasabi sold abroad is actually horseradish dyed green. Real wasabi is a rare, hard-to-grow plant.

q: Which fermented soybean paste is the base of a famous Japanese soup?
x: Miso is made by fermenting soybeans with salt and a mold called koji, sometimes with rice or barley added.

q: Which golden spice gives curry its yellow color?
x: Turmeric is the root of a plant in the ginger family. Its color comes from a compound called curcumin.

q: In a restaurant kitchen, what is 'mise en place'?
a: Having all ingredients prepared and in place
x: Mise en place is French for 'putting in place'. Chefs prepare everything before cooking starts.

q: Which Italian dessert layers ladyfingers soaked in coffee with mascarpone cream?
x: Tiramisu means 'pick me up' in Italian, a nod to the caffeine in the coffee-soaked cookies.

q: Which fruit, often treated as a vegetable, is the main ingredient of ketchup?
x: Tomatoes are botanically fruits. Early ketchups were made from mushrooms, walnuts or fish instead.

q: Which French pastry is shaped like a crescent and made of buttery layers?
x: The croissant's flaky texture comes from folding butter into the dough again and again, a process called lamination.

q: Which pastry is made of choux dough, filled with cream and topped with icing?
x: Choux pastry puffs up in the oven with no yeast or baking powder, using only steam.

q: Which delicate French sandwich cookie comes in pastel colors and is made with almond flour?
x: A good macaron has a smooth shell and a ruffled edge at its base, called the 'foot'.

q: Which sweet pastry is made of thin phyllo layers, chopped nuts and syrup?
x: Baklava is popular from Greece and Turkey to the Levant, and a good one can have 30 or more layers of phyllo.

q: Which Spanish fried-dough pastry is often dipped in thick hot chocolate?
x: Churros are piped through a star-shaped nozzle, which creates their signature ridges.

q: Which U.S. holiday is traditionally celebrated with roast turkey and pumpkin pie?
x: Thanksgiving is celebrated on the fourth Thursday of November in the United States.

q: At Spain's yearly food-fight festival in Buñol, what do people throw?
x: La Tomatina has taken place on the last Wednesday of August, and trucks bring in over a hundred tons of ripe tomatoes.

q: Which hard Italian cheese is traditionally grated over pasta?
x: Real Parmigiano Reggiano is aged for at least a year and carries a stamp of origin on its rind.

q: Which spice comes from the inner bark of a tree and is rolled into quills?
x: As the bark dries, it curls into the familiar rolled sticks. It has been traded for over 4,000 years.

q: Which tropical fruit is the signature topping on Hawaiian pizza?
x: Despite the name, Hawaiian pizza was invented in Ontario, Canada, by a Greek-born restaurateur in 1962.

q: Which tart red berry is traditionally made into a sauce for roast turkey?
x: Cranberries grow on low vines in bogs, and farmers often flood the bog to harvest them as they float.

q: Which cereal grain is used to make tortilla chips and polenta?
x: Corn is also called maize. It was first domesticated in Mexico thousands of years ago.

q: Which type of lettuce is traditionally used in a Caesar salad?
x: Romaine leaves are sturdy enough to hold up to the thick dressing of a Caesar salad.

q: Which Indian dish layers rice with spiced meat or vegetables?
x: Biryani is cooked slowly, sometimes sealed with dough so the steam stays inside.

q: Which creamy sauce is made by whisking egg yolk and oil together?
x: Mayonnaise is an emulsion, which means tiny droplets of oil are held in suspension by the egg yolk.

q: Which vegetable is pickled to make gherkins?
x: Gherkins are small, bumpy cucumbers. The word comes from a Dutch term for 'little cucumber'.

q: Which leafy green vegetable made Popeye the cartoon sailor strong?
x: Spinach is a leafy vegetable that gets cooked down a lot: a big pile of raw leaves wilts to just a few spoonfuls.

q: Which part of a chicken is the drumstick?
x: Chicken legs have two parts, the drumstick and the thigh, and both are dark meat.

q: Which kitchen tool is used to beat eggs or whip cream?
x: A whisk's wire loops add air to a mixture, which makes it lighter and fluffier.

q: What do Americans call the fresh leaves of the coriander plant?
x: Cilantro is Spanish for coriander. Some people find it tastes like soap because of a genetic trait.

q: What are the individual segments of a garlic bulb called?
x: A bulb of garlic usually holds about ten to twenty cloves wrapped in papery skin.

q: Which fruit comes in varieties such as Granny Smith and Gala?
x: There are thousands of apple varieties worldwide, and they can range from very sweet to very sour.

q: Sushi rice is seasoned with which sour ingredient?
x: Vinegar was originally used to speed up the fermentation of sushi, and now it adds flavor to the rice.

q: Which fast cooking method uses a hot wok and constant tossing of the food?
x: Stir-frying cooks small pieces of food quickly over very high heat, keeping vegetables crisp.

q: Which kitchen tool is used to remove the skin of potatoes and carrots?
x: Swivel-blade vegetable peelers became common in the 1900s, which made kitchen prep much faster.

q: Which natural sugar is found in milk?
x: Lactose is made of two simpler sugars, glucose and galactose, joined together.

q: Which sour yellow citrus fruit is often squeezed over fish?
x: Lemon juice is acidic, so it can brighten flavors and also stops cut apples from turning brown.

q: Which sugary treat is made by spinning heated sugar into fine threads, often sold at fairs?
x: Cotton candy is called candy floss in Britain. A spinning machine forces melted sugar through tiny holes.

q: Which fruit is dried to make prunes?
x: Not every plum can be made into a prune. Only certain firm, high-sugar varieties dry well without fermenting.

q: Which everyday seasoning is harvested by evaporating seawater or mined from underground?
x: Humans have used salt for thousands of years, and it was once so valuable that it was used as money.

q: Which dark, salty condiment is brewed from fermented soybeans and wheat?
x: Soy sauce originated in China more than 2,000 years ago and later became a staple of Japanese cooking.
